references.text: The preceding part of the parable of the Good Samaritan, which provides context for verse 35 where the Samaritan pays for the injured man's continued care.
Jesus' conclusion to the parable where he asks who was a neighbor to the beaten man and urges the listener to do likewise – this follows directly after the Samaritan's care in verse 35.

The command to open your hand wide to the needy and willingly lend them what they need reflects the Samaritan's generosity in paying for the injured man's care and promising to cover further expenses.

The command "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" is the very foundation of the entire parable of the Good Samaritan, and the Samaritan's practical love in verse 35 is a concrete illustration of this commandment.

In the parable of the minas, a nobleman gives money to his servants with the expectation that they will manage it until he returns – a similar pattern where someone entrusts resources with responsibility to another person until their return.

Paul teaches that love is the fulfillment of the law, and that whoever loves their neighbor has fulfilled the law – the Samaritan's act of paying for the injured man's care is a practical example of such neighborly love.
John urges us not to love with words alone, but in deed and truth – the Samaritan's concrete financial sacrifice for the injured man's care illustrates precisely this kind of practical love.
James warns against saying "go in peace" without providing what is necessary for the body – the Samaritan does the opposite by ensuring concrete material help and payment for further care.

"Do not withhold your help from the needy when it is within your power to give it" – the Samaritan's willingness to pay for the injured man's care and promise to cover more upon his return is a practical example of this wisdom.
